items.title: PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw Enabling Root Privilege Escalation and VM Escape
items.summary: A public proof of concept for Vghost, a high-severity Linux vhost flaw tracked as CVE-2026-74580, shows how the bug can let a local user gain root access or, in certain virtual machine setups, break out of a guest and affect the host. The issue has a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8 and is fixed in updated Linux kernel releases. Vhost is a Linux kernel system that helps virtual machines handle network and other device traffic more quickly. It uses shared virtual queues, called virtqueues, to carry device data between a guest and the host. The flaw lies in how vhost caches IOTLB mappings used to find those queues in memory. The problem occurs when a virtual ring is reconfigured. Linux updates the ring’s address or size but doesn’t clear the cached mapping for the ring’s descriptor, available, or used data. A later cache hit can therefore skip the expected address check and translate the new address using an old mapping. The resulting pointer may reach kernel copy routines with an invalid target. Researchers on the Seclists mailing list traced the bug to two earlier kernel changes: one introduced the metadata cache, while the other deferred guest I/O address validation. PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw For local privilege escalation, an attacker first needs permission to open a vhost device such as /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. The PoC primes the cache, changes a ring address without clearing the cached entry, then triggers the queue. The researchers say this can read and write kernel memory. The demonstrated chain uses a kernel memory read to work out the address randomization offset, then writes to the kernel’s modprobe_path setting. Triggering a kernel module request can then run an attacker-controlled helper with root privileges. The researchers report reproducing the chain on Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. Device permissions differed: the tested Ubuntu system limited access to the kvm group, while the other listed test systems exposed the device to ordinary users. That difference makes device permissions an important exposure check, but it does not replace patching. Membership in kvm or another group with access to vhost devices should be treated as privileged while a system remains unpatched. The second path starts inside a virtual machine. It requires a vhost device using a virtual IOMMU, iommu_platform, and the virtio queue-reset feature VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. A guest can reset and re-enable a queue, leading the host to reconfigure its ring while the stale metadata remains cached. When the guest then triggers the queue, the stale mapping can send a used-ring write beyond guest memory and into the QEMU process heap. The researchers say the corruption can crash QEMU or affect its control flow. This is a configuration-dependent VM escape risk, not a claim that every virtual machine can be escaped through the flaw. The upstream fix clears the vring metadata cache when the ring address or size is changed, so the new configuration must pass IOTLB validation. The first fixed upstream stable releases listed for the affected series are 5.10.265, 5.15.216, 6.1.183, 6.6.152, 6.12.104, 6.18.45, 7.1.9, and 7.2. Administrators should install a fixed kernel or a vendor backport and reboot into it. Until then, restrict access to all vhost device nodes, including /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*. Do not pass these devices to untrusted containers. For unpatched virtualization hosts, avoid exposing vhost devices with iommu_platform behind a virtual IOMMU to untrusted guests. Permission changes do not revoke file descriptors that are already open, and they do not address the guest-triggered path. For related coverage, see Cyber Security News’ reports on Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws and KVM guest-to-host escape risks . The technical analysis and PoC are available from Tencent Zhuque Lab and GitHub. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Inside Hyperdrive: How we solved a rare Hyperdrive MySQL caching bug
items.summary: Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive , Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support. We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat. During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works. What is Hyperdrive? Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database. Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections. For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive. A journey to stability Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake and we negotiate utf8 as the encoding. As it turns out, utf8 is a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1-3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use utf8mb4 , which fixed the emoji issue. Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION . This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to latin1 , once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of latin1 . The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset. A hard-to-find bug During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces. But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching. Hyperdrive caching To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache. Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint. MySQL client/server protocol Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol . Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues. The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server. This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase , where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command. Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior. This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects. While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js ( mysql2 ) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it. While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required. After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities. Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other. Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios. Endpoint caches, Client reads The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache. Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive. Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities. This diagram shows that flow: Client caches, Endpoint reads Client is finishing serving a request for query Q, and it writes the translated response bytes R_worker to cache. Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for Q, and checks the cache to find R_worker. Endpoint sends R_worker to a different Client, and this Client tries to translate R_worker to the Worker’s capabilities, and ends up sending an early EOF or hangs. You can see that here: Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%. Reliability is a feature You can use Hyperdrive support for MySQL today! Create a Hyperdrive to an existing MySQL-compatible database via the dashboard or wrangler, or connect to a new PlanetScale database . If you run into any issues or have questions, reach out on our Discord . npx wrangler hyperdrive create HYPERDRIVE_NAME --connection-string="mysql://user:password@db-host.example.com:3306/dbname"

Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive, Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support.

We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat.

During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works.

What is Hyperdrive?

Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database.

Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections.

For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive.

A journey to stability

Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake and we negotiate utf8 as the encoding. As it turns out, utf8 is a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1-3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use utf8mb4 , which fixed the emoji issue.

Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION. This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to latin1, once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of latin1. The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset.

A hard-to-find bug

During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces.

But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching.

Hyperdrive caching

To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache.

Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint.

MySQL client/server protocol

Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol. Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues.

The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server.

This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase, where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command.

Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior.

This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects.

While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js (mysql2) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it.

While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required. 

After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities.

Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other.

Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios.

Endpoint caches, Client reads
  1. The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache.
  2. Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive.
  3. Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities.

This diagram shows that flow:

Client caches, Endpoint reads
  1. Client is finishing serving a request for query Q, and it writes the translated response bytes R_worker to cache.
  2. Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for Q, and checks the cache to find R_worker.
  3. Endpoint sends R_worker to a different Client, and this Client tries to translate R_worker to the Worker’s capabilities, and ends up sending an early EOF or hangs.

You can see that here:

Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%.

Reliability is a feature

You can use Hyperdrive support for MySQL today! Create a Hyperdrive to an existing MySQL-compatible database via the dashboard or wrangler, or connect to a new PlanetScale database. If you run into any issues or have questions, reach out on our Discord.

items.title: FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used to Infiltrate U.S. Companies
items.summary: The FBI disrupted several U.S. laptop farms used by North Korean threat group FAMOUS CHOLLIMA in late September 2026, cutting off infrastructure that helped fake remote workers enter American companies. CrowdStrike disclosed the joint operation on October 13, describing it as the start of a wider effort against the group’s domestic support network. The farms housed company laptops that overseas operatives controlled remotely while posing as U.S. employees. This setup helped them hide their locations, collect salaries for North Korea’s regime, and keep access to employer systems. CrowdStrike said dozens of affected organizations operated across aerospace, energy, finance, healthcare, cybersecurity, defense engineering, government technology, and consumer technology. CrowdStrike researchers identified false identities, technical indicators, and U.S. computers supporting the scheme between April 2025 and June 2026. Their report on the disruption describes remote access tools and hardware abuse, not a newly identified malware family. The team combined device activity with targeted investigations to uncover local facilitators and share findings with the FBI. FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used The operation depended on a simple gap: a worker hired under a stolen identity could not easily receive a company laptop abroad without raising questions. As earlier reporting on North Korean identity fraud explains, local helpers provide the addresses and equipment needed to make overseas workers appear domestic. CrowdStrike observed operatives filing false police reports claiming laptops had been stolen, then requesting replacements at farm addresses. Others claimed sudden moves to redirect deliveries or rotated through residential addresses to hide the final destination. Some obtained jobs through IT staffing firms, allowing client devices to reach farms without those firms knowing. Once a laptop arrived, a facilitator added hardware and software for remote control. The physical device stayed in the United States while its operator worked elsewhere. This local presence helped the group pass location checks, handle employer equipment, and support identity and financial checks needed to receive wages. The farms also supplied a trusted local presence for financial checks. CrowdStrike described facilitators as providing a physical address, a legal identity, and a route through bank due diligence requirements. That makes the support network more than a place to store laptops: it connects hiring, access, and payment. Taking a farm offline forces operators to rebuild that chain, even when the wider group can move elsewhere. Device Spoofing Complicates Detection Since May 2026, CrowdStrike has observed FAMOUS CHOLLIMA spoofing device hashes, including making a video capture card appear to be a webcam. Researchers also saw the same disguised device across separate victim organizations, suggesting operators reused device identifiers while trying to avoid detection. Farm networks shared identifiers across several fake worker identities at the same time, offering another clue to coordinated activity. The findings complement earlier coverage of remote interview fraud tactics , where stand-ins and remote desktop tools helped hide who was actually completing interviews and technical work. The distinction matters for defenders: a legitimate tool can support an illegal operation without being malware. CrowdStrike names Astrill VPN, AnyDesk, OBS Studio, and PiKVM as technologies to review in context. Their presence alone does not prove compromise, but unexplained use alongside identity or shipping inconsistencies deserves investigation. CrowdStrike recommends standard background checks and reviews for reused phone numbers, email addresses, bank accounts, resume wording, and website content across profiles. Other warning signs include differences between identity documents and video appearances, suspicious job references, new public profiles, and login activity inconsistent with a worker’s claimed location. The FBI disrupted several U.S. laptop farms used by North Korean threat group FAMOUS CHOLLIMA in late September 2026, cutting off infrastructure that helped fake remote workers enter American companies.

CrowdStrike disclosed the joint operation on October 13, describing it as the start of a wider effort against the group’s domestic support network.

The farms housed company laptops that overseas operatives controlled remotely while posing as U.S. employees. This setup helped them hide their locations, collect salaries for North Korea’s regime, and keep access to employer systems.

CrowdStrike said dozens of affected organizations operated across aerospace, energy, finance, healthcare, cybersecurity, defense engineering, government technology, and consumer technology.

CrowdStrike researchers identified false identities, technical indicators, and U.S. computers supporting the scheme between April 2025 and June 2026.

Their report on the disruption describes remote access tools and hardware abuse, not a newly identified malware family. The team combined device activity with targeted investigations to uncover local facilitators and share findings with the FBI.

FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used

The operation depended on a simple gap: a worker hired under a stolen identity could not easily receive a company laptop abroad without raising questions.

As earlier reporting on North Korean identity fraud explains, local helpers provide the addresses and equipment needed to make overseas workers appear domestic.

CrowdStrike observed operatives filing false police reports claiming laptops had been stolen, then requesting replacements at farm addresses.

Others claimed sudden moves to redirect deliveries or rotated through residential addresses to hide the final destination. Some obtained jobs through IT staffing firms, allowing client devices to reach farms without those firms knowing.

Once a laptop arrived, a facilitator added hardware and software for remote control. The physical device stayed in the United States while its operator worked elsewhere.

This local presence helped the group pass location checks, handle employer equipment, and support identity and financial checks needed to receive wages.

The farms also supplied a trusted local presence for financial checks. CrowdStrike described facilitators as providing a physical address, a legal identity, and a route through bank due diligence requirements.

That makes the support network more than a place to store laptops: it connects hiring, access, and payment. Taking a farm offline forces operators to rebuild that chain, even when the wider group can move elsewhere.

Device Spoofing Complicates Detection

Since May 2026, CrowdStrike has observed FAMOUS CHOLLIMA spoofing device hashes, including making a video capture card appear to be a webcam.

Researchers also saw the same disguised device across separate victim organizations, suggesting operators reused device identifiers while trying to avoid detection.

Farm networks shared identifiers across several fake worker identities at the same time, offering another clue to coordinated activity.

The findings complement earlier coverage of remote interview fraud tactics, where stand-ins and remote desktop tools helped hide who was actually completing interviews and technical work.

The distinction matters for defenders: a legitimate tool can support an illegal operation without being malware. CrowdStrike names Astrill VPN, AnyDesk, OBS Studio, and PiKVM as technologies to review in context.

Their presence alone does not prove compromise, but unexplained use alongside identity or shipping inconsistencies deserves investigation.

CrowdStrike recommends standard background checks and reviews for reused phone numbers, email addresses, bank accounts, resume wording, and website content across profiles.

Other warning signs include differences between identity documents and video appearances, suspicious job references, new public profiles, and login activity inconsistent with a worker’s claimed location.

The latest disruption follows earlier nationwide laptop farm searches reported in June 2025, but the operations should not be treated as the same case. CrowdStrike did not disclose an exact farm count, arrest total, or seized device count for the September 2026 action.

CrowdStrike warned that the disruption will likely have a limited local effect rather than stop the wider operation.

items.title: Update Windows: Record Patch Tuesday fixes flaw already under attack
items.summary: Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday release addresses a record-breaking 1,413 vulnerabilities , including an actively exploited Windows Shell zero-day and two other publicly disclosed flaws. Just when you thought a previous record would stand for a while, Microsoft comes out again with the largest monthly Patch Tuesday release. Microsoft has said its growing use of AI to find and fix security vulnerabilities means users should expect more fixes in its monthly updates. How to apply patches and check if you’re protected These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date: Click the Start button, then open Settings . Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left). Click Check for updates . Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options , you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update. Otherwise, continue to the next step. If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update. After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date , you’re all set. Technical details As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details. We’ll start with the actively exploited vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-96951 ( CVSS score 8.8 out of 10), a Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability. The security feature it can bypass is the Mark of the Web (MOTW) defense, which can warn users about potentially unsafe downloaded files. Successful exploitation requires user interaction. For example, in an email or instant message attack, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file designed to exploit the vulnerability, but the user would have to click a link or open an attachment. Another one to keep an eye on is CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS score 8.8 out of 10), where an untrusted search path in .NET Framework allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally. The bypassed feature is Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC), which could lead to the ability to run unauthorized applications on target systems. This vulnerability was publicly disclosed before the patch. Another publicly disclosed vulnerability is CVE-2026-92707 (CVSS score 5.3 out of 10). The flaw can let an unauthenticated remote attacker exhaust memory in affected applications that process specially crafted MessagePack data. MessagePack-CSharp is a software component that helps applications pack and unpack data in a compact format, making it efficient to store or exchange information. Exposure depends on how a service uses the library to pack and unpack the information. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. items.title: Fake Calendly “Meta Careers” pages steal Facebook and Google logins
items.summary: We found a wave of websites posing as Calendly booking pages for job interviews at Meta. Visitors pick a slot for a 30-minute phone call with a recruiter, fill in their details, and pass what looks like a CAPTCHA. Then the page asks them to log in to Facebook. The interview is fake. The pages are designed to steal the visitor’s Facebook login details, including the two-factor authentication (2FA) codes meant to protect the account. Visitors are then asked to sign in to their Google account too, supposedly “for security.” These pages are not affiliated with Meta, Calendly, or Google. If you’ve already entered a password or approved a sign-in prompt, secure the affected accounts straight away. See “How to stay safe” below. Why Calendly makes a convincing disguise Calendly is a widely used scheduling tool, and recruiters use it to book interviews. Clicking a booking link, picking a time, and typing in your name and email is something people do without a second thought. There’s no account to create and nothing to download. That routine makes it a good disguise. By the time the page asks for something unusual, the visitor has already picked a slot and shared their details. Going along with one more step can feel easier than starting to doubt the whole thing. For someone who has sent out application after application without hearing back, an invitation to interview at Meta may be exactly the kind of message they hope for. Excitement, and the fear of missing a rare chance, can push people to move quickly instead of checking who actually sent the link. Job seekers are also used to sharing personal details with strangers. Handing your name, email, and phone number to a recruiter you’ve never met is a normal part of applying, so a form asking for them may not raise any alarms. A job interview that starts with a calendar The fake page copies Calendly’s booking screen, titled “Calendly | Meta Careers.” It shows a monthly calendar, a time zone picker, and a 30-minute “Phone call.” The available times are loaded from the attackers’ server, so the calendar looks like a real recruiter’s schedule. After the visitor picks a time, the page walks them through a series of steps: Your details. A form asks for your name, email address, and phone number, plus anything that “will help prepare for our meeting.” A fake CAPTCHA. A grid of images asks you to “Select all images with…”. It makes the page feel legitimate, and it may also stop automated security scanners from seeing what comes next. A Facebook login. A window within the page copies Facebook’s login page. It even draws its own fake address bar showing a Facebook web address, so it looks like a genuine browser pop-up. The copy comes complete with realistic error messages such as “The login information you entered is incorrect.” The page also asks visitors to sign up for a “Career Profile.” Your Facebook security code. If the account has 2FA, the page asks for the code from your authentication app, text message, WhatsApp, or email. A Google sign-in. The page claims “Facebook requires you to sign in to the Gmail address” on your account. To make the request seem harmless, the page adds that “Facebook will not share any of your data with your Google Account.” Fake Google screens, again under a fake address bar, ask for your password and then whatever Google asks for: a tap on a phone prompt, a code from Google Authenticator, a text message code, or your recovery email address. Everything you type into these screens, including the Google password, is sent to the attackers’ collection server. A fake confirmation. Finally, the page says a calendar invitation has been sent and that you’ll hear back within 90 minutes. By the time you start wondering, the attackers may already be inside your accounts. How the scam can get past two-factor authentication Many phishing pages simply collect a password and stop. This one keeps going. While the visitor is on the page, it keeps checking in with the attackers’ server and waits to be told which screen to show next. That allows the attackers to try the stolen password on the real Facebook site right away. If Facebook asks for a code, the fake page asks the visitor for the same code, and the attackers can use it before it expires. If the code doesn’t work, the page simply says “Incorrect code. Please try again.” The Google screens support the same approach. If Google sends a sign-in prompt to the visitor’s phone, the fake page can tell them to “tap Yes,” potentially approving the attackers’ login. The visitor sees the fake page while the attackers attempt to sign in to the real service out of sight. Codes and phone prompts still make accounts much harder to take over, so keep them turned on. But a code entered into a fake page, or a prompt approved for someone else’s login, can let attackers in. Passkeys and compatible hardware security keys are tied to the genuine website, so a fake page like this cannot relay them in the same way. That protection won’t help if you instead choose a password-and-code fallback and give those details to the attackers. Signs of a reusable phishing kit The code carries a version number ( 0.8.0 ), detailed error logging, and a “campaign key” sent with every message to the attackers’ server. These features suggest a reusable kit with support for identifying different campaigns. The collection address uses Amazon API Gateway in AWS’s Singapore region, ap-southeast-1 . A comment left in the code is written in Vietnamese. It translates to: “Change the key here when deploying to production.” Neither the hosting region nor the language of a code comment establishes who is behind the pages or where they operate. Facebook accounts, especially those linked to business pages or ad accounts, are valuable to criminals. Taking over the Google account as well could expose email and other data, and let attackers reset passwords for accounts linked to that address. The domains are another warning sign. All 11 follow the same pattern: join plus a recruiting-sounding word, such as joinhire , joinquest , or jointheteam , on the .cfd , .info , and .works top-level domains. None mention Calendly or Meta. These generic names could also be reused for other companies’ job lures. How to stay safe Check the address, not the design. Direct Calendly booking links use calendly.com , although legitimate forms can also be embedded on other websites. Treat an unfamiliar recruiting domain as a reason to verify the invitation independently. Don’t give a booking page your Facebook password. Scheduling a call doesn’t require handing your social media password to a recruiter. If a booking flow suddenly asks you to sign in elsewhere, verify both the request and the actual login domain. Look at your browser’s real address bar. These fake login windows draw their own address bars showing Facebook or Google web addresses. For a separate pop-up, check the address displayed by the browser itself. A login window that cannot be dragged outside the webpage may be part of the page rather than a separate browser window. Verify the recruiter and role. Go directly to the company’s official careers site. A genuine job listing doesn’t prove the person contacting you represents the company, so verify unexpected invitations through an independent contact. Don’t share codes or approve unexpected prompts. Only enter a code on the genuine service for a login you initiated. Never approve a phone prompt just because a recruiter or booking page tells you to. Use passkeys or a security key where you can. They resist this kind of phishing. Be wary if a page pushes you to use a password and code instead. Already entered a password or approved a prompt? From a trusted device, go directly to the affected service and change your password. Sign out other sessions and check your security methods, recovery email, and phone number. If both accounts were affected, secure your Google account promptly because email access can help attackers reset other passwords. Check Gmail for unfamiliar forwarding rules and filters, and review any Facebook business pages or ad accounts you manage. Change the password anywhere else you reused it. Locked out of your account? Use Meta’s account recovery support or Google’s compromised-account gui d ance . If you only shared contact details, watch for follow-up scams that use them to sound convincing. items.title: Package managers have an integrity problem
items.summary: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded. Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. Acknowledgments Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎ Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎ cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl , but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎ A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact . As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎ Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎ Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎ Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎ The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile . Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎
