I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed1, fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded.

Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits2, are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions.

One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table.

Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures.

The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for:

 * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock.
 * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted.

The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated.

This is documented behavior, and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation6.

Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected.

Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++.

"requires": [
 "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337"
],

This includes the package name (zlib), the version number (1.3.1), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20, and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash.

The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency.

SPEC CHECKSUMS:
 Files: d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a

This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec, which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository.

"source": {
 "git": "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git",
 "tag": "4.0.2"
},

So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag.

Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt.

"dist": {
 "type": "zip",
 "url": "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c",
 "reference": "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c",
 "shasum": ""
},

However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer.

Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity

The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example.

Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm, pnpm, Poetry, uv, and Yarn), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo).

Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches.

The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation.

Signatures are common; verification is not

Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem.

Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM7. The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity.

Repository signing

One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure.

Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry, the NuGet Registry, and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys. NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys. The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time.

Developer signing

Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader.

There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers. RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed.

The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA, and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys.

One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key.

Identity-based signing

An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore. Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature.

Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing8. GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code.

Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI, the npm Registry, RubyGems repository, and Maven Central. While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys.

Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent

Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers.

In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install. Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures, which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command, but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command.

In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept, which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source. These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers.

Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys (gem cert --add) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification, which works similarly.

Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip, uv, and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability, this verification code was removed. Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not9. At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.”

Go package management and transparency logs

Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package10, it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database. The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes.11

Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities, the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior.

Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key.

A proposed cryptographic design for package managers

One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity.

With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys.

This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification, the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata, and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it.

It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality.

One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality.

Acknowledgments

Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security.

  3. cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl, but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎

  4. A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎

  5. Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎

  6. Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test, call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub. ↩︎

  7. The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification.   8. Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎

items.title: VirusTotal Integrates Threat Intelligence With ChatGPT for Malware Analysis
items.summary: VirusTotal can now bring threat intelligence into ChatGPT through VirusTotal AI (VTAI), allowing users to investigate suspicious files, URLs, domains, and IP addresses within a conversation. The connection helps analysts retrieve existing reports and explain detection results while keeping the source, analysis date, and coverage visible. The integration uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that connects AI tools with external services. VirusTotal’s ChatGPT connection guide describes setup through Developer mode and an OAuth connection. Users sign in with Google through VTAI without supplying a VirusTotal API key. Availability depends on account and workspace settings. VirusTotal ChatGPT Integration For an explicitly authorized ChatGPT attachment, the connector can fetch and hash the original file content. It checks whether VirusTotal already knows that hash before uploading anything. Known files return existing reports, while only confirmed unknown files are submitted. Creating the connection alone does not prove attachment support works. This approach separates report retrieval from file contribution. Retrieving an existing report consumes query quota, including repeated lookups and analysis status checks. At Cybersecuritynews, we have successfully integrated VirusTotal with ChatGPT to enhance our analysis capabilities. Recently, we conducted an in-depth check on a PDF file, and here are the results. VirusTotal GPT Analysis (Source: Cybersecuritynews.com) Uploading a confirmed unknown file does not spend that quota, although separate contribution limits apply. Receipt recovery is free, helping users resume interrupted work without resubmitting the same sample. VirusTotal can now bring threat intelligence into ChatGPT through VirusTotal AI (VTAI), allowing users to investigate suspicious files, URLs, domains, and IP addresses within a conversation.

The connection helps analysts retrieve existing reports and explain detection results while keeping the source, analysis date, and coverage visible.

The integration uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that connects AI tools with external services. VirusTotal’s ChatGPT connection guide describes setup through Developer mode and an OAuth connection. Users sign in with Google through VTAI without supplying a VirusTotal API key. Availability depends on account and workspace settings.

VirusTotal ChatGPT Integration

For an explicitly authorized ChatGPT attachment, the connector can fetch and hash the original file content. It checks whether VirusTotal already knows that hash before uploading anything.

Known files return existing reports, while only confirmed unknown files are submitted. Creating the connection alone does not prove attachment support works.

This approach separates report retrieval from file contribution. Retrieving an existing report consumes query quota, including repeated lookups and analysis status checks.

At Cybersecuritynews, we have successfully integrated VirusTotal with ChatGPT to enhance our analysis capabilities. Recently, we conducted an in-depth check on a PDF file, and here are the results.

VirusTotal GPT Analysis (Source: Cybersecuritynews.com)

Uploading a confirmed unknown file does not spend that quota, although separate contribution limits apply. Receipt recovery is free, helping users resume interrupted work without resubmitting the same sample.

For network investigations, users can request URL submissions or domain and IP reanalysis when authorized. Keeping each request identifier helps track the registered analysis after an interruption.

These checks extend workflows covered in Cyber Security News’ VirusTotal threat research guide, bringing report review into a conversational interface.

The connection also builds on VirusTotal’s earlier use of AI, including Code Insight for malware analysis. However, threat report access should not be mistaken for a final security verdict.

Missing reports mean the result is unknown. Pending analysis and zero detections do not establish that a file or website is safe.

Privacy remains a concern. Standard submissions share content with VirusTotal and may expose it to security community members and partners. Analysts should obtain permission before submitting personal documents, internal code, credentials, or sensitive data.

Complete submitted URLs can disclose information carried in query strings and fragments, making review before submission essential. According to the VTAI overview, access is free within quotas. Permissions and allowances apply across account connections, not per chat.

For security teams, the benefit is easier access to evidence, not a replacement for investigation. Analysts still need to assess report age, coverage, and context before deciding whether to block, isolate, or escalate.

items.title: Police receive fake murder tip from Anthropic’s Claude AI
items.summary: Police tip hotlines already have their fair share of crank callers. Apparently they now have to contend with crank AI agents as well. AI agents have already been caught hacking software companies , breaching an Australian government portal , and trying to hack a Canadian government website . Now Anthropic’s Claude has added a made-up murder tip to the list. Claude’s Haiku 4.5 model filed a false tip in an unsolved Philadelphia homicide via the police department’s online public tip form, Anthropic disclosed . The tip was flagged as spam and didn’t reach investigators. AI’s latest “what does this button do?” moment happened during an internal test on randomly chosen web pages, the company said. Claude submitted the tip on July 18 at 11:27 pm through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, according to police. Tips submitted there can inform real homicide investigations. A fabricated account could send investigators chasing something that never happened. Here’s what Claude Haiku wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” The agent didn’t provide any description of the person that it didn’t actually see. Neither did it leave any contact details before hitting submit. Haiku did this as part of Anthropic’s internal testing. It had to invent and perform sample tasks on random web pages with live internet access so the company could see how it behaved. There was a list of prohibited actions to go along with the test. Anthropic told the agents not to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit “anything destructive.” The instructions did not explicitly rule out form submissions. The spam filter caught this one. Philadelphia police said the report never reached its Real-Time Crime Center for review or distribution to investigators. The department did not explain why it was flagged as spam. All tips go through human review before going out to investigators. That safeguard limited the impact of the incident, the department said, but did not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting made-up information as though it came from someone with knowledge of a crime. As it put it in a statement : “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers.” Anthropic discovered the false tip on September 28 and notified police on October 7, according to the department. Police called the two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable.” It is coordinating with the City Law Department, its Office of Innovation and Technology, and the Mayor’s executive team, the department added. Anthropic described the real-world impact of the incidents in its report as minimal. It has now disabled live internet access across its internal evaluations until it confirms that its safeguards reliably catch this behavior. The company said the transcript suggested Haiku was just trying to produce example content rather than trying to deliberately mislead the cops. But it also admitted that we can’t completely rely on a model’s account of its own reasoning. That leaves its explanation provisional, however reassuring it might sound. An allowlist could offer a tighter boundary for tests like these, limiting agents to approved sites and actions. A live police tip form should hardly be a testing ground. The homicide tip was not the only unwanted submission. Anthropic noted that federal, state, and local government websites also got visits from Claude, which repeatedly tried to fill out forms. Although Anthropic didn’t go into detail, a State Department official said that it got 20 visa applications from a testing model (19 in August, and one in May). None of them were processed, the official added. When an AI gives you fake information about who Beyoncé is married to, it might be irritating but it might only affect your team’s fortunes in a trivia night. The stakes get much higher when we’re dealing with intelligence that can inform law enforcement actions or public policy. In August, the head of the UK’s Police AI center warned law enforcement there to pause plans for AI use in criminal justice work. This came after the UK’s West Midlands Police apologized to members of Parliament over false evidence involving an invented soccer match. The error arose from the use of Microsoft Copilot. Anthropic’s latest incident raises a further concern: AI agents can put invented information into real systems themselves. What would happen if someone deliberately sent agents to flood police tip lines? This time, the false account stayed in spam. The people relying on those tip lines deserve safeguards that hold up when the next submission gets through. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. items.title: Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability Enables Privilege Escalation Attacks
items.summary: Microsoft has released fixes for a Windows SmartScreen vulnerability that allows an attacker with local access to gain higher privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-85851, the flaw was disclosed on October 13, 2026, and carries a CVSS base score of 7.8. Microsoft rates it Important. The issue involves a use-after-free memory error and affects several Windows 11 releases and Windows Server 2025. According to the supplied Microsoft advisory, successful exploitation lets an attacker move from a low integrity level to a medium integrity level. This is a specific increase in access, not a confirmed path to administrator or SYSTEM privileges. The attacker must already have low privileges on the affected device, but the attack requires no user interaction. The flaw falls under CWE-416, use-after-free . This error occurs when software continues to access memory after that memory has been released. Another operation may reuse the same memory, leaving the original code working with data that no longer belongs to it. Such errors can cause memory corruption, crashes, or other security problems. Microsoft identifies local privilege escalation as the impact for this vulnerability. Its CVSS vector lists low attack complexity, low privileges required, and no user interaction. Those conditions describe an attacker who already has a foothold on the device, not someone exploiting SmartScreen directly over the internet. Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability Microsoft credits researcher yhw with reporting the issue. At publication, the advisory marked it as neither publicly disclosed nor exploited and assessed exploitation as “Exploitation Less Likely.” Those findings do not remove the need to patch, but they do not support describing this flaw as an actively exploited zero-day. Earlier SmartScreen attacks involved different weaknesses. Cyber Security News previously covered SmartScreen bypass attacks delivering malware through CVE-2024-21412 and Water Hydra’s SmartScreen zero-day campaign . Those reports concern bypassing security warnings and should not be confused with the newly disclosed local privilege escalation flaw. Microsoft also disclosed CVE-2026-83504 , a Windows SmartScreen information disclosure flaw rated CVSS 4.7 and classified as a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition. An attacker who successfully exploits this second flaw could view heap memory from a privileged process. Exploitation requires winning a race condition, which explains its high attack complexity. It also requires local access and low privileges and needs no user interaction. Microsoft credits its Offensive Research & Security Engineering team and reports no exploitation at publication. The supplied material does not establish an exploit chain between the two flaws. For CVE-2026-85851 , the supplied update list covers Windows 11 versions 23H2, 24H2, 25H2, 26H1, and 26H2 across x64 and ARM64 systems. Windows Server 2025, including Server Core, is also listed. The listed fixes are KB5126653 for Windows 11 23H2, KB5127648 for 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2, KB5127646 for 26H1, and KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025. Administrators should match each device to its release and architecture, then verify installation against Microsoft’s update records. The two advisories list different update packages, so check their patch details separately before deploying across affected systems. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits Can Fully Compromise iPhones From a Single Web Visit
items.summary: Two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, show how a visit to a malicious or compromised website can put an outdated device at risk. The kits can link several software flaws together to break out of the browser and reach deeper parts of iOS. Depending on the device’s software version and the kit used, an attacker may then steal sensitive information without needing the user to install an app or tap through extra prompts. These are not ordinary malicious webpages. An exploit kit is a set of tools that checks a visitor’s device and selects code designed for its software. Coruna contains five complete exploit chains and 23 exploits targeting iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1. DarkSword uses a six-flaw chain against iOS 18.4 through 18.7. The two kits target different iOS ranges, so the risk depends on the version installed. Researchers from iVerify identified and studied DarkSword with Google and Lookout, and iVerify has also reported on newer variants in the wild. In an investigation published in October 2026, its researchers described a modified strain called P7 DarkSword, which can steal keychain and cryptocurrency wallet data. Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits The attack starts when Safari loads a malicious page or content hidden inside a compromised website. The page checks the iPhone’s model and iOS version, then serves code suited to that device. A WebKit or JavaScriptCore flaw can let the code run in the browser. Further flaws help it escape the browser’s safety limits and gain higher system access. That chain matters because the browser normally runs in a restricted area called a sandbox. A sandbox is designed to limit what a webpage can reach. Coruna and DarkSword use additional flaws to break past those limits; the later stages can reach kernel-level access, which gives the attacker much broader control over the device. Earlier Coruna exploit research describes the range of exploits and iOS versions involved. The tools can then collect valuable data. Reporting on DarkSword describes theft of passwords, messages, browsing records, location information and cryptocurrency wallet contents. iVerify’s P7 analysis adds on-device keychain collection and two-way communication with the attacker’s server. That information can put both personal accounts and work access at risk, especially when the phone holds saved credentials or is used to approve sign-ins. From targeted tools to wider criminal use Coruna’s history shows how a powerful exploit can move between different users. Google tracked its use from a surveillance customer to espionage activity against Ukrainian users and later to financially motivated campaigns using fake finance and cryptocurrency websites. The kit’s final payload, called PlasmaLoader, is designed to target cryptocurrency wallets and search Apple Notes for recovery phrases. DarkSword also moved beyond limited use after its source code was leaked publicly in 2026. That made the kit easier for other attackers to obtain and adapt. Separate reporting has described attackers combining DarkSword’s route into a device with Coruna’s wallet-theft tools, a development covered in this DarkSword and Coruna platform report . A public leak does not mean every copy works on every iPhone, but it can make reuse and changes easier. The threat can be difficult to spot. Some implants run inside normal system processes and may remove parts of their activity when finished. Browser or network monitoring can also miss what happens after the exploit code reaches the device. iVerify reported that some DarkSword variants leave useful traces, including Safari history and crash logs, while Coruna artifacts may remain after a reboot or iOS update. Installing the latest iOS update available for the device is the most important step. Updates close known flaws used in these chains; Apple has also issued security fixes for older supported devices. Users should check Settings for Software Update and install the version offered for their model. Lockdown Mode can provide extra protection for people at higher risk, but it is not a replacement for updates. It works best when enabled before opening a malicious page and can limit some features. Users should also avoid signing in through unexpected finance or cryptocurrency pages, even when a site looks familiar. Organizations should track iOS versions across work devices, review which accounts each phone can access and have a plan to isolate a suspected device for investigation. If compromise is suspected, treat credentials stored on that phone as exposed: change them from a trusted device, revoke active sessions where possible and involve the organization’s security team. A loaner phone can help staff keep working while investigators preserve the original device. items.title: Security vendors are racing to govern AI agents. Are they protecting the right thing?
items.summary: BigID and Varonis, two of the larger companies in data security, have both shipped products in the last couple of months aimed at the same problem: AI agents getting to company data. BigID launched AgentIQ on September 21. It lets customers run their data security and compliance work from a prompt or an AI agent, either inside BigID or from assistants like Claude, Copilot, GPT, and Gemini. According to BigID, agents working through AgentIQ inherit the permissions of the person who asked, and every action they take is logged. Varonis announced Agent Intent-Based Access Control in August as part of its Atlas platform. It compares what an agent was told to do with what the agent actually does: the tools it calls, the data it opens, and its reasoning along the way. If the agent drifts from its instructions, Atlas can alert on it, block the action, or quarantine the identity behind it. I think both are well engineered, and both companies are responding to a real problem. Agents now open files, call tools, and pass work to other agents, and most of the access controls companies have in place today were designed for people. Both products control the agent Based on what each company has published, the two products take the same basic approach. They limit what an agent is allowed to do, record what it does, and step in when it does something it wasn’t asked to do. Dimension BigID AgentIQ Varonis Atlas Agent IBAC What it covers Agents doing data security and compliance work through BigID Agents connected to enterprise data How it limits an agent The agent inherits the requesting person’s permissions The agent’s actions are checked against the instruction it was given What it records Every action, tied back to a person Every action and its intent, across the whole session What happens when something’s wrong Access stays limited to what the person could do Alert, block, or quarantine the identity Two kinds of agents Most of the agents people use today work on someone’s behalf. Copilot is one example, and so is an agent working through AgentIQ. They run with the permissions of the person using them, so if that person can open a file, the agent can open it too. Other agents run under their own identity. A company sets them up with a service account or another machine identity and gives them their own access, separate from any one person. They often run without anyone watching in real time, and some are started by other agents. The difference matters because the risks aren’t the same. An agent working for a person can surface anything that person has access to, including files they forgot they could open. An agent with its own identity can reach whatever it was granted, and that access is easy to set too broadly and hard to keep track of. What controls on the agent leave open Controls on the agent decide what an agent is allowed to do, and they make those decisions before or during the request. They don’t change what the data looks like once an agent is allowed to open it, or once one gets to a file through access that was set too broadly. For an agent working on someone’s behalf, what matters is how much that person can reach in the first place. For an agent with its own identity, what matters is whether the files it reaches can be read at all. I’m not saying agent governance is wasted effort. Knowing which agents exist and what they’re doing is useful, and it isn’t something PKWARE does. But it works on the agent, and neither of those problems gets solved without also working on the data. What’s in the rest of this series Part 2 looks at what protecting the data does for each kind of agent, and where it stops. Part 3 turns that into five questions to ask a data loss prevention (DLP) or data security posture management (DSPM) vendor before you buy. items.title: Hackers Breach Meta GitHub Repositories, Steal Source Code and Data of 1,500 People
items.summary: Hackers used an employee’s stolen credentials to access some of Meta’s GitHub repositories, taking product source code and personal information linked to roughly 1,500 people. Most affected individuals are Meta employees in the United States, according to the company’s disclosure to SecurityWeek. Meta confirmed the breach on October 13, 2026, when it began notifying affected people. The company said it detected the intrusion several weeks earlier, blocked the attackers’ access, and brought in GitHub and law enforcement to support its response. Stolen Credentials Opened Repository Access Meta said attackers entered through stolen employee credentials, not a flaw in a Meta product. The company also said its internal systems were not breached. The disclosed incident involved business data held in GitHub repositories. The report does not explain how the credentials were stolen or identify the attackers. Meta said its investigation with GitHub had not indicated that the group specifically targeted Meta’s data. That assessment remains based on the investigation so far. According to Meta, 99% of the stolen material was business data, consisting of software code related to some products. Personal information accounted for the remaining 1%. Those percentages describe the stolen material, not the share of employees affected. Meta has not named the affected products or detailed the repository contents. The disclosure does not say that attackers changed code, published it, or used it to compromise other systems. Meta told SecurityWeek it mistakenly placed personal information in the repositories, despite company rules that prohibit storing it on GitHub. items.title: Attackers Breach European Bank Through Third-Party Gateway and Target WSUS Server
items.summary: A European bank was breached through a poorly secured, third-party gateway before an attacker tried to exploit its Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) infrastructure. The case shows how stolen login details and weak access controls can put a bank’s central software systems at risk without a complex attack chain. The bank’s security team uncovered unauthorized VPN access attempts stretching across several months after spotting unusual activity on its central IT system. Investigators traced the intrusion to an external gateway managed by a third party, where strict authentication had not been properly enforced. Researchers from Unit 42 identified the intrusion and its attempted code execution, but their report does not name any malware family. Published on October 13, 2026, the investigation describes an opportunistic attacker whose noisy actions exposed basic security gaps rather than a confirmed, advanced spying operation. Attackers Breach European Bank The attacker used compromised credentials to sign in to internal systems through the gateway. Unit 42 did not name the appliance vendor or explain how those credentials were first obtained. The confirmed entry point was weak authentication on the externally managed device, not a disclosed gateway software exploit. That distinction matters because valid accounts can give an intruder access without requiring a new vulnerability. Earlier reporting on brute-force attacks against VPNs describes separate incidents involving weak passwords and appliances lacking multifactor authentication, showing why remote access settings deserve close review. Those incidents are not linked to this bank. Once inside, the intruder repeatedly scanned hosts and networks across several protocols, interacting with thousands of systems. Instead of quietly following one narrow path, the attacker searched broadly for more opportunities to gain access. Unit 42 said the volume of scanning and use of common system identifiers showed little effort to stay hidden. Over several months, the attacker also ran repeated password-guessing campaigns against internal systems, with administrator accounts a key focus. These attempts sought additional access while the intruder explored the environment. Separate coverage of automated VPN login attacks illustrates how repeated credential testing can threaten remote access services, although the bank’s reported password guessing occurred internally. The activity extended beyond logins. Automated web requests scraped internal pages and attachments, while the attacker searched operational and network shares. This exposed documentation during the intrusion. However, the report does not give a stolen data volume, identify affected customers, or confirm that customer banking records were taken. WSUS Exploit Attempt Stopped The attacker later targeted a remote code execution vulnerability in WSUS on the bank’s central configuration management server. That server handled software distribution across the organization, making it an attractive place to seek higher privileges and lasting access. Control of such a central service could have widened the incident’s impact. Unit 42 did not disclose the vulnerability’s CVE identifier. Although separate reporting on active WSUS vulnerability exploitation covers CVE-2025-59287, that identifier cannot be assigned to this bank incident from the published evidence. Keeping those cases separate avoids turning a related technical risk into an unsupported finding. Cortex XDR detected the attempt to run unauthorized code and contained the threat before it escalated. Unit 42 reported that the attacker was stopped from establishing persistent access or spreading further through the network. This containment followed earlier scanning, authentication attempts, and access to internal documentation; it did not prevent the initial breach. Responders reviewed endpoint records across thousands of systems and logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. They found no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors. Bank leaders reviewed the exposed documentation and rotated all compromised credentials. The bank also expanded its Cortex XDR and Cortex XSIAM coverage and incident response support. The investigation highlights authentication, timely patching, and endpoint detection as core safeguards. Third-party management did not remove the bank’s exposure to a weak gateway configuration, while containment and follow-up hunting helped limit the damage. For security teams, the lesson is to review vendor-managed access with the same care as internal systems. The report calls for strict identity controls, timely updates, and endpoint monitoring. Checking these controls together is important because a valid login can otherwise turn an outside gateway into internal access. items.title: Gears of War: E-Day Hit by DDoS Attack, Causing Login Failures and Disconnects
items.summary: Gear of War: E-Day players faced login failures, sudden disconnects, and other online service problems after distributed denial-of-service attacks targeted the game’s online services. The official Gears Community account confirmed the cause on X, linking the disruption to DDoS activity and ending speculation about the source of the failures. The Gears Community reported attacks on its online services that caused intermittent disconnects, login issues, and other disruptions, but did not identify the attackers, disclose traffic figures, or specify affected services, limiting details about the attack’s scale and method. A separate update from the same account said the login issue had been resolved and that the team would continue closely monitoring services. Earlier messaging had flagged extended login times and said the issue was improving. The updates show progress toward recovery, but the login fix should not be read as proof that every reported service problem had ended. Gears of War: E-Day Hit by DDoS Attack Players may experience delayed or failed logins, intermittent disconnections, and difficulty reconnecting, symptoms confirmed by the Gears Community during the online service disruption. The available statement does not establish that the attacker accessed player accounts or stole personal information. It describes an attack against service availability. Reporting the incident as a confirmed data breach would go beyond the evidence released by the Gears Community team. A DDoS attack uses multiple machines to overwhelm a target with traffic or requests. The aim is to make a system or network unavailable to legitimate users. Compromised devices can form a botnet, allowing attackers to send traffic from many sources at once, according to CISA’s DDoS response guidance. This can exhaust network capacity or system resources, preventing the system from handling normal requests. However, the Gears update does not identify a botnet, a traffic flood type, or an attack rate. There is no published basis in that statement for assigning the incident to a known group or connecting it to another campaign. Gaming infrastructure has faced similar availability threats before. Cybersecurity News previously covered DDoS malware targeting Valve Source Engine game servers , with several supported attack methods. That report provides useful background on game-server threats. However, it does not link to the E-Day disruption. Another report examined a 3.15-billion-packets-per-second attack against a Minecraft server . The case shows why packet volume matters alongside bandwidth when assessing attacks. No comparable measurements have been shared in the available Gears statement. CISA recommends confirming DDoS activity through network monitoring and traffic analysis, then applying measures such as traffic filtering and rate limits. These are general defensive steps, not confirmed details of the Gears team’s response. Official updates confirm the reported cause, player impact, and login recovery, but leave the attack’s scale and technical handling undisclosed. The team’s stated recovery approach still includes monitoring after the service disruption. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Multiple Google Chrome Flaws Could Enable Memory Corruption and Code Execution Attacks
items.summary: Google released a Chrome security update that addresses 37 vulnerabilities, including seven critical flaws that raise concerns about memory corruption and possible code execution . Published on October 13, 2026, the update covers Windows, Mac, and Linux, with fixes spanning graphics, PDF handling, media processing, networking, and other browser components. According to Google’s Stable Channel Update for Desktop, the patched versions are 155.0.8059.79/.80 for Windows and Mac, and 155.0.8059.79 for Linux. The release includes seven critical, 29 high, and one medium-severity security fixes. Google says it will continue distributing updates over the coming days and weeks. The critical vulnerabilities include CVE-2026-110152, a buffer overflow in ANGLE, Chrome’s graphics translation layer. Zhenpeng “Leo” Lin at depthfirst reported the issue on September 30. Buffer overflows can corrupt memory when software writes beyond the space reserved for data, potentially creating opportunities for attackers to change program behavior. The remaining six critical entries are use-after-free flaws. CVE-2026-110149 affects Browser, CVE-2026-110136 affects PDF, CVE-2026-110161 affects Network, and CVE-2026-110165 affects Core. Multiple Google Chrome Vulnerabilities Google also patched CVE-2026-110148 in SVG and CVE-2026-110151 in Media. These findings involve Google researchers and Xinyang Ge. A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when software continues accessing memory after releasing it. Depending on the bug, attackers may influence that memory’s contents, causing crashes, corrupting data, or potentially running malicious code. However, the flaw category alone does not enable an attack against every affected component. Cybersecurity News previously covered Chrome’s update fixing 247 vulnerabilities , including four critical use-after-free issues. The latest release continues that focus on memory safety across multiple browser features rather than a single isolated component. Among the high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-110169 affects V8, Chrome’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine. Rapid7’s vulnerability record states that a crafted HTML page could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside Chrome’s sandbox in versions before 155.0.8059.79. That limitation matters. Code execution inside the sandbox does not, by itself, prove an attacker can take control of the entire operating system. items.title: A Little More Logic in Splunk: Introducing SPL2’s if Command
items.summary: A quick use case for the new execution flow control feature If you have spent enough time writing SPL (10y here!), you have probably run into a familiar situation: you want to process events differently depending on what they contain. In a typical SPL pipeline, commands are executed sequentially, and filtering commands such as where and search can reduce the number of events passed to subsequent commands. Maybe you want to enrich events conditionally, or apply different transformations based on a field value. In classic SPL, you can often get the job done with eval, if(), case(). That works, but what if you want to control which block of code gets executed based on a field’s value, just as you would in a procedural programming language ? Enter SPL2’s if command. How does it work? The SPL2 if command was announced for Splunk Cloud Platform version 10.5.2605 on June 29, 2026, but I only became aware of it after seeing this LinkedIn post from Mikael Bjerkeland : SPL vs. SPL2: what actually changes? One important distinction: SPL already has an if() function . You do not need SPL2 to write conditional expressions. In classic SPL, you might use: | eval severity=if(status>=500, "high", "medium") The SPL above evaluates a condition and returns one of two values. For several conditions, you might use case()function. This is present in pretty much any modern piped language, including KQL . SPL2's if command works differently. Instead of using conditional logic only to calculate a value via eval, it lets you define different processing paths directly in your search. In other words: you can control which SPL2 statements or code blocks are executed based on a condition. It is a small feature, but one that can make certain searches more powerful. A real use case: to enrich or not to enrich? If you have ever worked with events containing network IP addresses, you probably know about the challenges of enriching them with geolocation. The problem becomes more significant in a large enterprise environment, where network traffic comes from all over the globe. In Splunk there's a command called iplocation which allows users to enrich the IP address value with its corresponding geolocation data (country, latitude, etc). This has become important enough that many vendors now include this enrichment in their logs. That's the case for Azure/Entra Sign In logs. The logs contain a field called location that holds a two-letter country code linked to the IP origin. However, for whatever reason, not every IP address gets enriched, as you can see below: 30-min worth of sign-in events sorted by most prevalent countries So, what's the solution here? Enrich it yourself, right? A quick use case for the new execution flow control feature

If you have spent enough time writing SPL (10y here!), you have probably run into a familiar situation: you want to process events differently depending on what they contain.

In a typical SPL pipeline, commands are executed sequentially, and filtering commands such as where and search can reduce the number of events passed to subsequent commands.

Maybe you want to enrich events conditionally, or apply different transformations based on a field value. In classic SPL, you can often get the job done with eval, if(), case().

That works, but what if you want to control which block of code gets executed based on a field’s value, just as you would in a procedural programming language?

Enter SPL2’s if command.

How does it work?

The SPL2 if command was announced for Splunk Cloud Platform version 10.5.2605 on June 29, 2026, but I only became aware of it after seeing this LinkedIn post from Mikael Bjerkeland:

SPL vs. SPL2: what actually changes?

One important distinction: SPL already has an if() function. You do not need SPL2 to write conditional expressions.

In classic SPL, you might use:

| eval severity=if(status>=500, "high", "medium")

The SPL above evaluates a condition and returns one of two values. For several conditions, you might use case()function. This is present in pretty much any modern piped language, including KQL.

SPL2's if command works differently. Instead of using conditional logic only to calculate a value via eval, it lets you define different processing paths directly in your search.

In other words: you can control which SPL2 statements or code blocks are executed based on a condition.

It is a small feature, but one that can make certain searches more powerful.

A real use case: to enrich or not to enrich?

If you have ever worked with events containing network IP addresses, you probably know about the challenges of enriching them with geolocation.

The problem becomes more significant in a large enterprise environment, where network traffic comes from all over the globe.

In Splunk there's a command called iplocation which allows users to enrich the IP address value with its corresponding geolocation data (country, latitude, etc).

This has become important enough that many vendors now include this enrichment in their logs. That's the case for Azure/Entra Sign In logs.

The logs contain a field called location that holds a two-letter country code linked to the IP origin.

However, for whatever reason, not every IP address gets enriched, as you can see below:

30-min worth of sign-in events sorted by most prevalent countries

So, what's the solution here? Enrich it yourself, right?

The issue is that if you decide to fill the gap (location = Unknown) with enriched data returning from the iplocation command, you need to do it for every single IP address, not only for the unknown ones.

In SPL, that would look like this:

In this case, iplocation is executed for every single IP value, no matter what!

As you can imagine, looking up the geolocation of every IP address can become expensive, depending on the use case (hunting, reporting, etc.) and the event volume (or lookback period). The query may end up running much more slowly than necessary.

The SPL2 solution

With the if command, users can run iplocation only on events where the location field is empty (condition).

Based on the example, the SPL2 code equivalent would look like this:

SPL2 query leveraging the 'if' command to selectively use the 'iplocation' command

A few notes here:

  • This is a common demand, especially when pivoting to ASN hunting to reveal threat actor infrastructure from a specific location.
  • The iplocation command doesn't produce a two-letter country code, but you can enrich or normalize the result later using public lists.
  • If you leverage Data Engineering or Data Pipelines, it's worth enriching critical data sources such as Entra ID at ingestion time.
Closing: is that a big deal?

I haven’t had much time to explore this further, but I’m sure I’ll come across other use cases. For now, I wanted to share this with the community and hear what others think.

That’s likely not the best example, but perhaps better than the one in the reference docs which can be easily done using SPL's eval…

A few more interesting examples:

To be transparent, I rarely use SPL2, and I suspect many detection engineers and threat hunters are in the same boat. However, some of its features can be particularly useful in specific scenarios.

There are pros and cons to using it that deserve a deeper discussion, so perhaps I’ll explore those in a future article.

items.title: Critical Vulnerabilities Discovered in Google Chrome and Arm GPU Drivers
items.summary: Florian Schweitzer, Security Researcher at Certitude Consulting, has identified two serious vulnerabilities in products from Google and Arm that affect the same attack vector in the GPU software stack used by modern web browsers and mobile devices (CVE-2026-9034 and CVE-2026-93374). The issue can be triggered via JavaScript and could enable a sandbox escape. Such vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to compromise a user’s device after they visit a website. The discovery comes at a time of significant changes in vulnerability research, driven by the increasing use of artificial intelligence. The starting point for Schweitzer’s research was a deliberate decision not to compete with the enormous computing resources already being used to identify vulnerabilities in Chrome. “My strategy was simple: If you can’t compete with Google’s computing resources, you shouldn’t even try. I wanted to find attack surfaces that are difficult to integrate into a fuzzer or a fully automated AI workflow: real devices, stateful behavior, and boundaries between systems,” Schweitzer explained. Nevertheless, Schweitzer made extensive use of AI to generate WebGPU workloads, create automated test harnesses and device instrumentation, modify and compile Chromium, process crash data, and assist with reverse engineering the proprietary GPU driver. Rather than treating the model’s conclusions as definitive answers, he followed a process inspired by Austrian philosopher Karl Popper: formulating competing hypotheses, turning them into experiments, and attempting to falsify them as early and cost-effectively as possible. “The economics become interesting when the cost of failure decreases. If a hypothesis that would previously have taken several weeks to test can now be tested and discarded within a few hours, security researchers can conduct significantly more experiments. The competitive advantage increasingly lies in deciding which questions are worth asking, which evidence can be trusted, and which results warrant another hour of investigation,” said Marc Nimmerrichter, Managing Partner at Certitude Consulting. Critical Chrome Vulnerabilities Compared: 2025 and 2026 Certitude’s analysis of Google’s public Chrome Stable security releases shows that only four critical Chrome vulnerabilities were fixed in 2025. Three of these were reported by external security researchers, while one was attributed to Google. As of September 17, 2026, the same public data lists 179 critical vulnerabilities fixed in 2026: 145 attributed to Google and 34 to external researchers. External researchers have therefore already contributed more than ten times as many critical findings as in the previous year. At the same time, the number of critical findings attributed internally to Google has increased from one in 2025 to 145 in 2026. This shift coincides with Google’s rapid expansion of AI use in security research. In July, the Chrome Security Team described this as a “massive shift in the software security industry” and explained that large language models enable automated vulnerability discovery on a scale beyond traditional human research. Google states that it now uses AI throughout the entire vulnerability lifecycle, including vulnerability discovery, reproduction, triage, and remediation. The first vulnerability reported by Schweitzer, CVE-2026-9034, affects the Arm Mali GPU userspace driver. According to the public security advisory, an unprivileged process executing valid GPU operations “via WebGL or WebGPU” could access previously freed memory. The vulnerability affects several generations of Arm GPU drivers, including the 5th Gen GPU architecture, which provides graphics and compute capabilities for a wide range of consumer devices, including smartphones, tablets, TVs, and wearables. The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-93374, affects Google Chrome. Google classifies it as critical and describes it as a “use after free in Dawn,” Chromium’s implementation of WebGPU. The public CVE description identifies the issue as remotely exploitable via a crafted HTML page and as a potential sandbox escape: “Use after free in Dawn in Google Chrome on Android prior to 153.0.8010.52 allowed a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Critical)” Potential Sandbox Escape The Chrome sandbox is a key security boundary designed to restrict access to the underlying operating system by exposed browser components responsible for rendering websites. Vulnerabilities that can bypass this boundary are therefore particularly dangerous. Exploit code can be delivered via a link to a website. Google credits Florian Schweitzer with reporting the Chrome vulnerability on April 8, 2026. Arm also publicly names Schweitzer of Certitude Consulting as the discoverer of CVE-2026-9034. Detailed technical information is intentionally being withheld during the coordinated disclosure process to avoid providing information that could enable exploitation before affected systems are adequately protected. Further details will be published at an appropriate time. items.summary: Microsoft has patched an actively exploited Windows Shell zero-day vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web protections. Tracked as CVE-2026-96951, the flaw was addressed in the October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates . It carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and is rated Important by Microsoft. The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before the update, but Microsoft confirmed that exploitation had already occurred. Its “Exploitation Detected” assessment signals a confirmed attack rather than a possible future threat. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index advises customers to give applicable updates in this category the highest priority. Windows Shell 0-Day Exploited The flaw involves command injection, where Windows Shell fails to properly handle special elements used in a command. Microsoft describes the outcome as a security feature bypass available to an unauthorized attacker over a network. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to evade Mark of the Web defenses. Mark of the Web identifies files that come from the internet and helps Windows apply warnings or other protective checks. Bypassing this protection can remove an important barrier between a downloaded file and a user opening dangerous content. However, the reported impact is a security bypass, not a standalone remote code execution flaw. Attackers can deliver a specially crafted file through email or instant messaging and use social engineering to persuade the target to open it. Exploitation requires user action. This means the flaw should not be treated as a zero-click attack, despite its network-based delivery path. Earlier reporting on Windows LNK Stomping attacks described another way attackers bypassed Mark of the Web through Windows shortcuts. Separately, a WinZip Mark of the Web vulnerability showed how archive extraction could lose internet-origin tags.
